title: Interior skin focusing and directional mirror transfer in a graded non-Hermitian Krawtchouk network
authors: Y. S. Liu, X. Z. Zhang
abstract: Spatially graded nonreciprocity can move skin weight away from a boundary, but it does not generally preserve a real commensurate spectrum or analytically controlled dynamics. We study a finite open Krawtchouk network with oppositely graded directed hoppings. For a broad intermediate range of asymmetries, their local imaginary gauge field changes sign in the bulk, and its accumulated coordinate generates a positive diagonal similarity map whose normalized squared entries form a biased-binomial envelope. The same map converts the open chain into the spin-rotation generator \(2gJ_x\), so the focus and equally spaced spectrum follow from one grading. In this focusing regime, exact right, left, and biorthogonal eigenvectors show that the envelope width and participation number both scale as \(\sqrt N\), identifying a subextensive interior focus. In the physical node basis, spin rotation produces perfect mirror inversion with direction-selective amplification and attenuation whose gains are mutually inverse. The directional Green functions share their poles, while their residues differ by the same similarity ratio. Closing the chain exposes a gauge-invariant imaginary flux, and either exact one-way limit yields an exceptional point of order \(N\). Onsite disorder preserves the directional resolvent ratio, whereas independent hopping disorder breaks the clean analytic Krawtchouk map and degrades commensurability and transfer. The model therefore provides an exactly solvable finite-network framework linking localization geometry and eigenvector nonorthogonality to commensurate spectra and node-resolved directional response.
summary: This paper analyzes a graded non-Hermitian Krawtchouk network to determine the conditions under which localized boundary effects (skin) can coexist with a perfectly regular, commensurate energy spectrum. By mapping the system to a Hermitian partner, the authors derive an exactly solvable model showing an interior focus scaling as $\sqrt{N}$. This framework is valuable for designing quantum systems with controlled, directional response and robust spectral properties.
main_problem: The study investigates the coexistence of an interior skin profile with a real commensurate spectrum, exact finite-time transfer, and analytic frequency-domain response in a finite non-Hermitian network.
main_result: The graded structure yields an exactly solvable framework demonstrating an interior focus scaling as $\sqrt{N}$, linking localization geometry to commensurate spectra and directional response.
method: The authors utilize a transformation to a Hermitian partner via a positive diagonal similarity map, analyzing spectral properties, directional propagators, and disorder effects.
model_or_system: The model is a finite open Krawtchouk network with oppositely graded directed hoppings, described by a non-Hermitian Hamiltonian $H_{OBC}$.
key_observables: Spectral half-width $B(r)$, conditioning curve $\log_{10} \kappa_S$, directional gain ratios, and the Petermann factor $K_\mu$.
important_parameters: System size $N$, grading parameters $\alpha_1, \alpha_2$, and disorder strengths.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the existence of a positive diagonal metric $\eta$ for pseudo-Hermiticity, and the comparison is made against the clean Krawtchouk map.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the graded gauge field, the similarity structure, mode-resolved eigenvector densities, and the approach to the one-way exceptional point by comparing spectral width and conditioning curves.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the graded structure and its link to a Hermitian partner, to analyzing directional dynamics and disorder robustness, and finally detailing the approach to the exceptional point using advanced asymptotic analysis.
why_interesting: The work provides an exactly solvable, analytically controlled framework for understanding how engineered non-Hermiticity can maintain spectral regularity and directional coherence despite complex boundary effects, which is highly relevant for designing robust quantum simulators or optical circuits.
